ASHEVILLE, North Carolina (CNN) -- In 1988, a relatively unknown rock and blues guitarist named Warren Haynes got some of his friends together to play music in Asheville, North Carolina. It was just an opportunity for local musicians to jam during the holidays, the one time of year they were all in town together. Warren Haynes' good work has been noted by the street named after him. The artists also wanted to give back to the community, so they gave the money raised by their show to various charities. The tradition has continued. Now celebrating its 20th anniversary, Haynes' Christmas Jam has evolved into an epic annual event for the musicians, fans, and particularly Habitat for Humanity. "We need Habitat For Humanity more now than ever, with the whole mortgage crisis that put us where we are now, and the fact that Habitat is about building homes for people that can't afford homes as opposed to lending money to people who can't afford homes," Haynes told CNN. Haynes and his wife, Stefani Scamardo, decided to donate 100 percent of the Christmas Jam proceeds to Habitat for Humanity years ago because they could see exactly where the money was going. They go back each year and meet the families they helped build homes for. Singer Joan Osborne echoed Haynes' thoughts. "It's a scary time. A lot of people are losing their homes so it's good to be able to do something that helps with that specific problem," she said. Going into 2008's shows, which were held December 12 and 13, the Christmas Jam had raised more than $665,000 for Asheville's Habitat For Humanity. The money has gone into building 12 houses in Enka Hills, a wooded community surrounded by mountains on a street the organization appropriately named Warren Haynes Drive. (In 2005 Habitat also built a house in the New Orleans Musicians Village.) The Thursday before the show, Haynes presented the key to a new home to single mother Suzie Cromer and her 8-year-old daughter. "Meeting the families and seeing the work that Habitat's doing with our help -- you know its hard to see that and not get emotional," Haynes said. "Warren is a hero in our mind," said Habitat's Arianne Kjellquist. "In western North Carolina, the housing costs are really out of whack with what the local wages are, so there's a big discrepancy there. There are more people that maybe would have been approved previously when the lending standards weren't so strict." This year's Christmas Jam lived up to the long-lasting and crowd-pleasing traditions of previous shows. The first night's show ran more than nine hours, ending with an Allman Brothers set after 4 a.m. The second night's show ended at 3:30 a.m. Performers included Ben Harper and Relentless 7, Travis Tritt, Michael Franti, Osborne, Ivan Neville's Dumpstaphunk, Steve Earle and Haynes' band Gov't Mule. Perhaps the most anticipated addition this year among both fans and artists was former Led Zeppelin member John Paul Jones, who played acoustic mandolin, bass and keyboards throughout the weekend with just about everyone. Jones said he was happy to pitch in. "In the economic climate like this, people really just want to get out and enjoy themselves and forget about the day to day stuff that they have to deal with. So it works on many levels," Jones said. "The fact that it is for a good cause is just a huge bonus." Haynes says the 20-year evolution of the Christmas Jam reflects his career. "We've grown up together. Its a parallel of the progress that I have achieved, and the event reflects not only the philosophy I share with these people but the mission." And as fans danced the night away while the artists played their hearts out, families' dreams of owning their perfect home come true. "I would have never imagined or dreamed that it would turn into what its turned into," Haynes reflected with a huge smile.

These funds have supported the construction of 12 houses in Enka Hills, a wooded community nestled among the mountains, on a street fittingly named Warren Haynes Drive. # The Warren Haynes Christmas Jam: 20 Years of Music and Charity in Asheville

What began as a simple holiday gathering among friends has blossomed into one of the most beloved charitable music traditions in the Southeast. In 1988, guitarist Warren Haynes, best known for his work with Gov't Mule and the Allman Brothers Band, invited a handful of fellow musicians to join him for an informal jam session in his hometown of Asheville, North Carolina. The idea was simple: bring together talented musicians during the holiday season for a night of impromptu collaboration and celebration.

That first gathering, held purely for the love of music and the camaraderie of the season, struck a chord with both performers and audiences alike. Word spread quickly, and what started as a casual get-together began attracting larger crowds and more prominent musicians each year. Recognizing the potential to give back to the community that had supported him throughout his career, Haynes transformed the event into a formal fundraiser, channeling the energy and goodwill generated by the music into meaningful charitable work.

Over the years, the Christmas Jam evolved to support various local charities, but its mission has since crystallized around a singular, powerful cause: Habitat for Humanity. Today, all proceeds from the event go directly toward building affordable housing for families in need throughout the Asheville area.

Now celebrating its 20th anniversary, the Warren Haynes Christmas Jam has become a fixture on the music calendar, drawing acclaimed artists from across genres who donate their time and talent to the cause. The impact has been substantial and measurable: the event has raised over $665,000 to date, funds that have directly translated into tangible results for the community.

Perhaps most remarkable is the physical legacy of this musical tradition. The proceeds have funded the construction of 12 homes in Asheville's Enka Hills community, providing safe and stable housing for families who might otherwise have struggled to achieve homeownership. In a fitting tribute to the event's origins and impact, these homes are symbolically located on a street named Warren Haynes Drive—a permanent reminder of how music can create lasting change.

The timing of this charitable work has proven especially significant given the broader economic context. As the housing and mortgage crisis swept across the United States, leaving countless families struggling with foreclosure, unstable housing situations, and diminished access to affordable homeownership, the Christmas Jam's contributions to Habitat for Humanity have provided crucial support precisely when it was needed most. While national housing markets faltered and families across the country faced uncertainty, the Enka Hills community stood as a testament to what grassroots charitable efforts, powered by music and community spirit, can accomplish even in challenging economic times.

What makes the Warren Haynes Christmas Jam particularly special is its authenticity—it remains rooted in the genuine musical passion that sparked it decades ago, while having grown into a sophisticated philanthropic engine. The event demonstrates how a simple idea, born from friendship and a love of music, can evolve into a lasting institution that provides real, measurable benefits to a community, one home and one holiday season at a time.

# Asheville: North Carolina's Mountain Gem

Nestled in the Blue Ridge Mountains of western North Carolina, Asheville has earned a reputation as one of the most captivating cities in the American Southeast. This vibrant city combines natural beauty, rich history, and a thriving arts and culinary scene that draws visitors from around the world.

## A City Surrounded by Nature

Asheville's location amid the Blue Ridge and Great Smoky Mountains gives it an unparalleled backdrop of forested peaks, winding rivers, and scenic overlooks. The Blue Ridge Parkway, often called "America's Favorite Drive," passes near the city, offering stunning vistas especially during autumn when the mountains explode with color. Nearby, the Great Smoky Mountains National Park provides endless opportunities for hiking, wildlife viewing, and outdoor adventure.

## Historic Architecture and Culture

The city is perhaps best known for the Biltmore Estate, America's largest privately owned home, built by George Vanderbilt in the late 19th century. This French Renaissance-style château, surrounded by manicured gardens and vineyards, remains one of North Carolina's top tourist attractions and offers a glimpse into the Gilded Age.

Beyond the Biltmore, Asheville's downtown showcases an impressive collection of Art Deco architecture, a legacy of a 1920s building boom. The city's compact, walkable core is filled with independent shops, galleries, and historic buildings that tell the story of its development.

## A Hub for Arts and Food

Asheville has cultivated a reputation as a haven for artists, musicians, and craftspeople. The River Arts District, a former industrial area along the French Broad River, now houses dozens of studios where visitors can watch artists at work and purchase everything from pottery to paintings.

The city has also become a nationally recognized culinary destination, earning nicknames like "Beer City USA" due to its concentration of craft breweries. Farm-to-table restaurants celebrate the region's agricultural bounty, while food trucks and eclectic eateries reflect Asheville's creative, independent spirit.

## Conclusion

Whether visitors come for outdoor recreation, architectural wonders, artistic inspiration, or culinary exploration, Asheville, North Carolina offers a distinctive blend of mountain charm and cosmopolitan flair that continues to capture the hearts of everyone who visits.

# Rock Legends Unite in Asheville for Holiday Charity Concert, Raising Funds for Habitat for Humanity

**ASHEVILLE, N.C.** — For nearly three decades, the mountains of Western North Carolina have come alive each December with the sounds of blues, rock and soul, as musicians from across the country descend on this small city for one of the most enduring traditions in the jam band world: Warren Haynes' Christmas Jam.

The annual concert, founded by Haynes — the Grammy-winning guitarist known for his work with the Allman Brothers Band, Gov't Mule and the Grateful Dead — has grown from a modest local gathering into a marquee event that draws thousands of fans and dozens of high-profile musicians to Asheville's US Cellular Center. But beyond the marathon sets and surprise collaborations, the Jam has built its legacy on a singular mission: raising money to build homes for families in need.

Since its inception, the concert has funneled millions of dollars to Habitat for Humanity of Asheville, funding the construction of numerous houses in the region. Organizers say the partnership reflects Haynes' desire to give back to the community that shaped his career, transforming a night of music into a lasting investment in affordable housing.

"This isn't just a concert — it's become a cornerstone of what the holidays mean here," said one longtime festival volunteer. "People come for the music, but they leave knowing they've helped put a roof over someone's head."

This year's lineup featured an eclectic mix of genres, with special guests joining Haynes and his band for extended jams that stretched late into the night. Surprise sit-ins and collaborative sets have become a hallmark of the event, with musicians often crossing genre lines to perform together for the first time.

Ticket sales, along with a silent auction featuring music memorabilia and VIP experiences, contribute directly to the Habitat for Humanity partnership. Organizers noted that in past years, the Jam has funded entire home builds, with families moving into their new residences shortly after the holiday season — a poignant echo of the concert's charitable spirit.

Local Habitat for Humanity officials have praised the long-running collaboration, noting that the funds raised provide critical support for a program that helps low-income families achieve homeownership through affordable mortgages and sweat equity.

For Haynes, who grew up in Asheville, the event remains deeply personal. He has spoken in the past about wanting to create something that outlasts a single performance — a tradition that continues to serve the community long after the final encore fades.

As the music died down early Sunday morning, organizers announced this year's fundraising total, adding to a legacy that has, over nearly 30 years, helped transform lives one home — and one song — at a time.

# Twenty Years of Harmony: How One Concert Built a Community

**RIVERSIDE** — When Mia Delgado picked up her guitar twenty years ago and invited a handful of friends to play a backyard benefit show, she wasn't thinking about legacy. She was thinking about the Hendricks family down the street, who'd lost their home to a fire and had nowhere to go.

"We raised $3,200 that first night," Delgado recalls, sitting in the same backyard where it all began, though the space now hosts a professional stage crew twice a year. "I thought that was incredible. I had no idea what it would become."

This weekend, that backyard concert has grown into "Chords for Homes," a two-day music festival that draws thousands of attendees and dozens of musicians—some now Grammy winners—who return year after year to honor where they started. Since its founding, the event has raised over $14 million and helped build 87 homes for families across the region.

## From Folding Chairs to Festival Grounds

The numbers tell one story, but the people tell another.

Marcus Chen was nine years old when his family moved into a home built with Chords for Homes funding after his father's construction accident left them struggling. Now 24, Chen returned this year not as an attendee, but as a volunteer stage manager.

"I used to just see musicians on a stage," Chen said. "Now I see neighbors. People who showed up for us before they even knew us."

That sense of reciprocity echoes throughout the festival grounds. Many of the volunteers handing out water bottles or directing parking are former recipients of homes built through the concert's proceeds. It's become something of an unspoken tradition—give back when you can.

## The Musicians Who Stayed

What makes Chords for Homes unusual in the world of charity concerts isn't just its longevity—it's its consistency. Several founding musicians, now in their fifties, still perform every year, turning down bigger-paying gigs to keep the commitment.

"There's a waitlist to play this show," laughed Del Rivera, a folk singer who's missed only one year since the beginning, due to surgery. "Artists want in. Not because it's glamorous—the stage is still kind of janky, honestly—but because you can see exactly where the money goes. That's rare."

That transparency has become part of the concert's identity. Attendees don't just donate; they tour completed homes, meet families, and hear directly from the carpenters and volunteers who build them alongside the charity's construction partners.

## Looking Forward

As the sun set on Saturday's opening night, Delgado took the stage one more time, guitar in hand, and did something she rarely does: she paused mid-set to introduce Elena Ruiz, a single mother of three who'll receive keys to her new home next month.

The crowd's cheer was less about the music and more about what the music had made possible.

"Twenty years ago, I thought I was throwing a concert," Delgado told the crowd. "Turns out, I was building a family. All of you are part of it."

As new luthiers and local artists join the growing bill each year, organizers say the event's future is secure—rooted not in nostalgia, but in the same simple idea that started it: neighbors helping neighbors, one song at a time.

# From Living Room Jam to Housing Lifeline: How One Musician's Holiday Tradition Built Homes

**RIVERSIDE** — What began fifteen years ago as an informal gathering of friends strumming guitars around Marcus Chen's fireplace has transformed into one of the region's most anticipated fundraising events, generating over $2.3 million for affordable housing initiatives since its inception.

The annual "Home for the Holidays" jam session, held each December at the Riverside Community Amphitheater, started humbly enough. Chen, former guitarist for the alternative rock band Static Bloom, simply wanted to gather musician friends for an evening of music during a particularly difficult winter.

"I'd just come back from touring, and half my crew was struggling to find stable housing between gigs," Chen recalled. "We weren't trying to save the world. We just wanted to play some songs and feel less alone during the holidays."

## From Fifteen Friends to Fifteen Hundred

What changed everything, according to longtime collaborator and bassist Ronnie Alvarez, was a conversation in 2015 that shifted the event's entire purpose.

"Marcus mentioned that three of the people playing that year didn't have permanent addresses," Alvarez said. "That hit different. We're musicians—we talk about struggle in our songs all the time, but here it was, sitting right next to us on stage."

The following year, Chen partnered with the nonprofit Riverside Housing Coalition, turning the gathering into a ticketed benefit concert. What started with 15 musicians performing for maybe 100 attendees has grown into a two-day festival featuring over 40 acts and drawing crowds exceeding 5,000.

Singer-songwriter Dana Whitfield, who has performed at the event for eight consecutive years, described watching the transformation firsthand.

"The first time I played, we were literally passing a hat around," Whitfield said. "Now we've got a full production team, and last year we funded an entire twelve-unit apartment complex. That's not a metaphor—there are actual families living in actual homes because people wanted to hear some music."

## Beyond the Music

The event's success has drawn attention from housing advocates nationwide, who point to it as a model for community-driven fundraising that doesn't rely solely on traditional charity structures.

"What makes this work is authenticity," said Patricia Nguyen, executive director of the Riverside Housing Coalition. "Marcus isn't a celebrity swooping in for a photo op. He's been showing up for this community for fifteen years, rain or shine, sold-out or not."

This year's lineup includes several artists who have benefited directly from housing assistance programs connected to the fund, including drummer Kai Morrison, whose family received support four years ago.

"I used to just watch this show from the crowd, wondering how we'd make rent," Morrison said, taking a break from soundcheck. "Now I'm on that stage playing drums. If that's not proof this thing works, I don't know what is."

## Looking Forward

Chen remains characteristically humble about the event's growth, insisting the mission hasn't changed even as the scale has.

"We're not curing homelessness," he said. "But if thirty musicians getting together can help build homes for thirty families, then multiply that by however many years we keep doing this—that adds up to something real."

# 35 Years of Giving: How Warren Haynes' Christmas Jam Built Homes and Community in Asheville

For nearly four decades, the mountains surrounding Asheville, North Carolina, have echoed each December with something more than holiday music—they've resonated with a mission that has fundamentally reshaped how the local music community thinks about giving back.

## A Local Show Becomes a Movement

What began in 1988 as a modest gathering of friends and fellow musicians has transformed into one of the most enduring charitable traditions in American music. Warren Haynes, the Grammy-nominated guitarist known for his work with the Allman Brothers Band, Gov't Mule, and as a member of the Grateful Dead's touring lineup, started the Christmas Jam simply as a way to bring together the musicians he'd grown up admiring and playing alongside in western North Carolina.

"It was never supposed to become this," Haynes has said in numerous interviews over the years, reflecting on how a hometown holiday concert evolved into a multi-night, arena-filling event drawing rock royalty from across genres.

The show quickly became known for its unpredictable, marathon-length jam sessions, with Haynes serving as ringleader—inviting guest after guest onstage for genre-crossing collaborations that might pair a bluegrass picker with a funk bassist or a blues legend with an up-and-coming singer-songwriter. That spirit of musical generosity mirrored the event's charitable core.

## Building More Than a Stage—Building Homes

While the music has always been the draw, the Christmas Jam's lasting legacy may be measured in something far more concrete: houses.

Since partnering with Habitat for Humanity of Asheville, the event has funneled significant proceeds directly into affordable housing construction in Buncombe County. Over the years, the Jam has helped fund the construction of numerous homes for local families, addressing a housing affordability crisis that has only intensified as Asheville's popularity as a tourist and retirement destination has driven up property values and pushed working-class residents further from the city center.

Organizers with Habitat for Humanity have repeatedly emphasized how unusual and valuable this kind of sustained, multi-decade partnership is. Rather than a one-time celebrity donation or a single benefit concert, the Christmas Jam has provided reliable, recurring funding that allows for long-term planning—a rarity in an industry often driven by one-off charity events.

Beyond housing, jam proceeds have also supported a rotating cast of other regional nonprofits over the years, including organizations focused on homelessness prevention, environmental conservation in the Blue Ridge Mountains, and music education programs for local youth.

## Musicians Return Year After Year

Part of what has sustained the Christmas Jam's charitable impact is its reputation among musicians as a genuine labor of love rather than a corporate obligation. Artists across generations and genres—from jam band royalty to country stars to indie rock acts—have made pilgrimages to Asheville each December, often performing for scaled-back fees or donating their time entirely.

Musicians who've played the event frequently describe it in similar terms: unpretentious, spontaneous, and rooted in genuine camaraderie rather than industry politics. The absence of rigid setlists and the encouragement of onstage improvisation have made it a favorite among musicians who relish the chance to play outside their usual bands and formats.

For Haynes himself, who still calls western North Carolina home, the event represents a direct line back to his roots—a chance to funnel the benefits of his career success directly back into the community that shaped him as a musician.

## A Model for Charitable Rock

As other artists have launched their own charitable concerts and festivals over the years, the Christmas Jam is frequently cited as something of a template: proof that a single artist's commitment to their hometown, sustained over decades rather than treated as a passing gesture, can produce measurable, lasting change.

With each passing December, as the guitars ring out and surprise guests take the stage in Asheville, the Christmas Jam continues to prove that a holiday tradition rooted in music can also lay literal foundations—one house, one family, and one community at a time.
